_comment: Guided tour for FRC resolution. Declarative AutoForm view (frc.view.json); steps target bound attributes and the custom sections' keys. The help page carries the long form -- these steps say which control decides the answer and in what order. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What this image resolves, not what the microscope could
steps.text:
Fourier ring correlation splits your acquisition into two independent halves, correlates them ring by ring in frequency space, and reports the frequency at which they stop agreeing.

Above that frequency the two halves contain different noise and nothing else — so it is the finest detail your data actually support, photon budget, drift and label included. It is a property of this acquisition, not of the instrument.

Five steps.

steps.title: Load the acquisition
steps.text: A frame stack, or a photon stream that will be binned into one. FRC needs many frames — the split has to leave enough photons in each half to form an image.

await.hint: Choose the image or photon file.

steps.title: The split IS the measurement
steps.text:
Everything rests on the two halves being independent measurements of the same object. Correlate an image with itself and you get 1 everywhere and no resolution; correlate it with a smoothed copy and you measure the smoothing.

Even/odd frames is the default, and both halves then span the whole acquisition so slow drift affects them equally.
First/second half is for detectors whose consecutive frames are not independent — or to ask whether the second half degraded.
Two channels means two detectors that saw the same structure. Not two labels on different structures: those correlate nowhere and the tool will report your field of view as the resolution.

That last failure is worth recognising, because it produces a number rather than an error.

steps.title: The criterion travels with the number
steps.text:
Fixed 1/7 (Nieuwenhuizen 2013) is the usual convention for fluorescence images. ½-bit (van Heel & Schatz 2005) and 2σ depend on how many Fourier pixels each ring holds — so they depend on the image size, and on the same data the three disagree by tens of per cent.

Quote which one you used. A resolution without its criterion is not comparable to anyone else's.

And set the pixel size: without it the answer is in pixels, and since the conversion is linear, an uncertain pixel size makes an equally uncertain resolution.

steps.title: Read the crossing — and know what no crossing means
steps.text:
The curve is the ring-by-ring correlation against spatial frequency; the resolution is where it drops through the threshold.

No crossing is a real answer, not an error. Either the halves agree at every frequency the sampling can show — the image is oversampled relative to its resolution — or they agree nowhere, which means too few photons, or a split whose halves were not independent.

Whichever number you get: more frames, a brighter label or a longer dwell all move it, because it describes the data and not the microscope. The ? button has the rest.
